claim: Dispositional greed is characterized by the insatiable hunger for more and the dissatisfaction for not having enough.
source: Dispositional greed, characterized by the insatiable hunger for more and the dissatisfaction for not having enough, has often been associated with heightened impulsivity and excessive risk-taking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a definition of dispositional greed, drawing from established understanding in the field.

claim: Dispositional greed has often been associated with heightened impulsivity and excessive risk-taking.
source: Dispositional greed, characterized by the insatiable hunger for more and the dissatisfaction for not having enough, has often been associated with heightened impulsivity and excessive risk-taking.
evidence: This is a general statement about existing associations in the literature, representing established knowledge.

claim: The exact neural mechanisms of how greed personality influences risk-taking are still ill understood.
source: Despite its far-reaching implications in social sciences and economics, however, the exact neural mechanisms of how greed personality influences risk-taking are still ill understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge, representing the state of the field.

claim: The correlation between subject's greed personality trait (GPT) score and risk-taking was selectively mediated by individual's loss aversion, but not risk attitude.
source: In the present study, we showed the correlation between subject's greed personality trait (GPT) score and risk-taking was selectively mediated by individual's loss aversion, but not risk attitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's behavioral analysis and mediation analysis.

claim: Gain and loss prospects were jointly represented in the activities of the ventral striatum and medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC).
source: In addition, our neuroimaging results indicated that gain and loss prospects were jointly represented in the activities of the ventral striatum and medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC).
evidence: This is supported by neuroimaging data from the fMRI experiment, specifically the conjunction analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mOFC responses encoded the neural loss aversion signal.
source: Furthermore, mOFC responses also encoded the neural loss aversion signal and mediated the association between individual differences in GPT scores and behavioral loss aversion.
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis showing correlation between mOFC activity and behavioral loss aversion, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: mOFC responses mediated the association between individual differences in GPT scores and behavioral loss aversion.
source: Furthermore, mOFC responses also encoded the neural loss aversion signal and mediated the association between individual differences in GPT scores and behavioral loss aversion.
evidence: This is supported by mediation analysis results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Recent development of greed research emphasizes two parallel facets in the operational definition of greed personality trait: the desire of always wanting more and the dissatisfaction of not having enough.
source: Interestingly, recent development of greed research also emphasizes two parallel facets in the operational definition of greed personality trait: the desire of always wanting more and the dissatisfaction of not having enough (Krekels and Pandelaere, 2015; Mussel and Hewig, 2016; Mussel et al., 2015; Seuntjens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent literature on greed research.

claim: Greed has long been considered a double-edged sword: it motives people to compete and outperform for better well-being, but is also associated with negative stereotypes such as immorality.
source: Greed has long been considered a double-edged sword: it motives people to compete and outperform for better well-being, but is also associated with negative stereotypes such as immorality (Livingstone and Lunt, 1992; Lunt and Livingstone, 1991; Piff et al., 2012; Rokeach, 1973; Seuntjens et al., 2016; Tickle, 2004; Vohs et al., 2006; Zandi, 2008) and excessive risk-taking which has been accused for insurmountable debt level and recent meltdown in the finance industry (Aquino et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on greed and its social implications.

claim: Greed is associated with excessive risk-taking which has been accused for insurmountable debt level and recent meltdown in the finance industry.
source: Greed has long been considered a double-edged sword: it motives people to compete and outperform for better well-being, but is also associated with negative stereotypes such as immorality (Livingstone and Lunt, 1992; Lunt and Livingstone, 1991; Piff et al., 2012; Rokeach, 1973; Seuntjens et al., 2016; Tickle, 2004; Vohs et al., 2006; Zandi, 2008) and excessive risk-taking which has been accused for insurmountable debt level and recent meltdown in the finance industry (Aquino et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on greed and financial crises.

claim: Current research demonstrating the association between greed personality trait and individual risk-taking is much less comprehensive and the results are inconsistent.
source: Although anecdotes and field studies generally suggest a potential link between greed personality trait and individual risk-taking, current research demonstrating this association is much less comprehensive and the results are inconsistent (Mussel et al., 2015; Seuntjens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature showing inconsistent findings.

claim: Self-assessed greed personality score was not related to risk-taking in a gain-only environment.
source: For example, it has been shown that the self-assessed greed personality score was not related to risk-taking in a gain-only environment (Seuntjens et al., 2015), while other studies tended to suggest that greed personality trait significantly influences individual's risky taking behavior.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seuntjens et al., 2015.

claim: Other studies tended to suggest that greed personality trait significantly influences individual's risky taking behavior.
source: For example, it has been shown that the self-assessed greed personality score was not related to risk-taking in a gain-only environment (Seuntjens et al., 2015), while other studies tended to suggest that greed personality trait significantly influences individual's risky taking behavior.
evidence: This is a general reference to other studies in the literature.

claim: Recent EEG studies showed reduced feedback-related negativity-difference to losses relative to gains in human subjects high in trait-greed.
source: In addition, recent Electroencephalography (EEG) studies also showed reduced feedback-related negativity-difference to losses relative to gains in human subjects high in trait-greed (Mussel and Hewig, 2016; Mussel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to EEG studies.

claim: Subjects' risk-taking is believed to be driven by their risk attitudes in the gain or loss only gambling tasks.
source: For instance, subjects' risk-taking is believed to be driven by their risk attitudes in the gain or loss only gambling tasks, but is influenced by both risk attitude and relative sensitivity towards gains versus losses (loss aversion sensitivity) in a gain-loss mixed gambling task.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prospect theory and decision-making literature.

claim: Risk-taking is influenced by both risk attitude and relative sensitivity towards gains versus losses (loss aversion sensitivity) in a gain-loss mixed gambling task.
source: For instance, subjects' risk-taking is believed to be driven by their risk attitudes in the gain or loss only gambling tasks, but is influenced by both risk attitude and relative sensitivity towards gains versus losses (loss aversion sensitivity) in a gain-loss mixed gambling task.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prospect theory.

claim: Under the theoretical framework of prospect theory, risk attitude (α) and loss aversion coefficient (λ) together determine the degree of risk-taking in a value-based gambling task.
source: This hypothesis can be formalized under the theoretical framework of prospect theory, where risk attitude (α) and loss aversion coefficient (λ) together determine the degree of risk-taking in a value-based gambling task (Barkley-Levenson et al., 2013; Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; Köbberling and Wakker, 2005; Tversky and Kahneman, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prospect theory literature.

claim: Individual greed personality trait might be related to the degree of loss aversion, but not risk attitude.
source: Therefore, extant literatures raise an intriguing possibility that individual greed personality trait might be related to the degree of loss aversion, but not risk attitude.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the literature review.

claim: Greed personality would only affect risk-taking in mixed gamble tasks, where loss aversion plays a role, but not in gain/loss only tasks, where loss aversion is not involved or canceled out.
source: It further predicts that greed personality would only affect risk-taking in mixed gamble tasks, where loss aversion plays a role (Mussel et al., 2015), but not in gain/loss only tasks, where loss aversion is not involved or canceled out (Seuntjens et al., 2016; Seuntjens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis and supported by citations.

claim: The activities of a network of brain structures, including ventral striatum, amygdala, and OFC, might encode a 'neural loss aversion' signal.
source: Previous research suggested that the activities of a network of brain structures, including ventral striatum, amygdala, and OFC, might encode a 'neural loss aversion' signal (Canessa et al., 2013; De Martino et al., 2010; De Martino et al., 2009; Park et al., 2011; Plassmann et al., 2010; Tom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: One significant concomitant personality trait often associated with greed is impulsivity.
source: Finally, given that one significant concomitant personality trait often associated with greed is impulsivity (Seuntjens et al., 2015) and impulsivity has been implicated to influence risk-taking (Baumann and Odum, 2012; Lejuez et al., 2003; Pack et al., 2001; Zaleskiewicz, 2001), we also measured subject's impulsivity trait score to dissociate it from the effect of trait-greed in risk-taking behavior.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seuntjens et al., 2015.

claim: Impulsivity has been implicated to influence risk-taking.
source: Finally, given that one significant concomitant personality trait often associated with greed is impulsivity (Seuntjens et al., 2015) and impulsivity has been implicated to influence risk-taking (Baumann and Odum, 2012; Lejuez et al., 2003; Pack et al., 2001; Zaleskiewicz, 2001), we also measured subject's impulsivity trait score to dissociate it from the effect of trait-greed in risk-taking behavior.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on impulsivity and risk-taking.

claim: Subjects' GPT and IPT scores significantly correlated with each other in the pilot questionnaires (r = 0.272, p = 0.018).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Seuntjens et al., 2015), we found subjects' GPT and IPT scores significantly correlated with each other in the pilot questionnaires (r = 0.272, p = 0.018) as well as in the fMRI dataset (r = 0.543, p = 0.005; Figure 2A), suggesting that IPT might be a confounding factor in identifying the specific effect of trait-greed (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pilot data.

claim: Subjects' GPT and IPT scores significantly correlated with each other in the fMRI dataset (r = 0.543, p = 0.005).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Seuntjens et al., 2015), we found subjects' GPT and IPT scores significantly correlated with each other in the pilot questionnaires (r = 0.272, p = 0.018) as well as in the fMRI dataset (r = 0.543, p = 0.005; Figure 2A), suggesting that IPT might be a confounding factor in identifying the specific effect of trait-greed (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IPT might be a confounding factor in identifying the specific effect of trait-greed.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Seuntjens et al., 2015), we found subjects' GPT and IPT scores significantly correlated with each other in the pilot questionnaires (r = 0.272, p = 0.018) as well as in the fMRI dataset (r = 0.543, p = 0.005; Figure 2A), suggesting that IPT might be a confounding factor in identifying the specific effect of trait-greed (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between GPT and IPT scores.

claim: The GPT score was significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in mixed trials (r = 0.440, p = 0.032).
source: Our data showed that the GPT was significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in the mixed gambles (r = 0.440, p = 0.032; Figure 2B), but not in gain (r = 0.236, p = 0.267; Figure 2C) nor loss only gambles (r = −0.002, p = 0.992; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The GPT score was not significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in gain trials (r = 0.236, p = 0.267).
source: Our data showed that the GPT was significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in the mixed gambles (r = 0.440, p = 0.032; Figure 2B), but not in gain (r = 0.236, p = 0.267; Figure 2C) nor loss only gambles (r = −0.002, p = 0.992; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The GPT score was not significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in loss only gambles (r = −0.002, p = 0.992).
source: Our data showed that the GPT was significantly correlated with the percentage of risky choices in the mixed gambles (r = 0.440, p = 0.032; Figure 2B), but not in gain (r = 0.236, p = 0.267; Figure 2C) nor loss only gambles (r = −0.002, p = 0.992; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Subjects' IPT scores were not correlated with the percentages of risky choices in all three-gamble contexts.
source: Furthermore, corroborating previous research that impulsivity was mainly related to the preference bias in the delay discounting tasks, our subjects' IPT scores were not correlated with the percentages of risky choices in all three-gamble contexts (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GPT might impact subjects' risk-taking only when both prospective gains and losses were presented (mixed trials) but not when single valence trials were involved (gain and loss only).
source: The discrepancy of correlation results between GPT and gambling percentages among three tasks implied that the GPT might impact subjects' risk-taking only when both prospective gains and losses were presented (mixed trials) but not when single valence trials were involved (gain and loss only).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of correlations observed in the data.

claim: According to the prospect theory model, individual risk-taking was driven solely by the risk attitude parameter (α) in the gain and loss only trials.
source: Importantly, according to the prospect theory model, individual risk-taking was driven solely by the risk attitude parameter (α, a constant representing valence sensitivity) in the gain and loss only trials, but by the interplay of both risk attitude (α) and loss aversion (λ, a parameter capturing the asymmetrical weighting of loss relative to gain) parameters in the mixed condition (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on the theoretical framework of prospect theory.

claim: According to the prospect theory model, individual risk-taking was driven by the interplay of both risk attitude (α) and loss aversion (λ) parameters in the mixed condition.
source: Importantly, according to the prospect theory model, individual risk-taking was driven solely by the risk attitude parameter (α, a constant representing valence sensitivity) in the gain and loss only trials, but by the interplay of both risk attitude (α) and loss aversion (λ, a parameter capturing the asymmetrical weighting of loss relative to gain) parameters in the mixed condition (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on the theoretical framework of prospect theory.

claim: People weigh losses more than gains.
source: Consistent with previous literature suggesting that people weigh losses more than gains (Chib et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2010; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2009; Tom et al., 2007), our results showed that the average loss aversion parameter (λ; mean = 1.561) across all subjects was significantly larger than 1 (t = 3.874, p = 0.001), implicating general loss aversion across subjects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by the current study's data.

claim: The average loss aversion parameter (λ; mean = 1.561) across all subjects was significantly larger than 1 (t = 3.874, p = 0.001), implicating general loss aversion across subjects.
source: Consistent with previous literature suggesting that people weigh losses more than gains (Chib et al., 2012; De Martino et al., 2010; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2009; Tom et al., 2007), our results showed that the average loss aversion parameter (λ; mean = 1.561) across all subjects was significantly larger than 1 (t = 3.874, p = 0.001), implicating general loss aversion across subjects.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model-derived parameters.

claim: Average risk attitude was not significantly different from 1 (mean = 1.033, t = 0.812, p = 0.425), indicating risk neutrality.
source: Average risk attitude was not significantly different from 1 (mean = 1.033, t = 0.812, p = 0.425), indicating risk neutrality (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model-derived parameters.

claim: Risk attitude and loss aversion parameters were not correlated (r = 0.020, p = 0.925).
source: Additionally, risk attitude and loss aversion parameters were not correlated (r = 0.020, p = 0.925).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of model-derived parameters.

claim: Subjects' loss aversion coefficients (λ) were negatively correlated with their GPT scores (r = −0.479, p = 0.018).
source: Our results showed that subjects' loss aversion coefficients (λ) were negatively correlated with their GPT scores (r = −0.479, p = 0.018; Figure 3A), but no correlation was found between risk attitude coefficients (α) and GPT scores (r = 0.062, p = 0.775; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No correlation was found between risk attitude coefficients (α) and GPT scores (r = 0.062, p = 0.775).
source: Our results showed that subjects' loss aversion coefficients (λ) were negatively correlated with their GPT scores (r = −0.479, p = 0.018; Figure 3A), but no correlation was found between risk attitude coefficients (α) and GPT scores (r = 0.062, p = 0.775; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Individual GPT score was specifically tied to loss aversion coefficient but not subject's risk attitude.
source: Thus, our model-based analyses confirmed previous behavioral results (Figure 2B–D) and suggested that individual GPT score was specifically tied to loss aversion coefficient but not subject's risk attitude.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of correlations observed in the model-based analysis.

claim: Participants' IPT scores were not correlated with α nor λ parameters of the model.
source: In contrast, participants' IPT scores were not correlated with α nor λ parameters of the model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between loss aversion coefficient and the percentage of risky gamble choice across all trials (r = −0.919, p < 0.001).
source: Furthermore, we found a significant negative correlation between loss aversion coefficient and the percentage of risky gamble choice across all trials (r = −0.919, p < 0.001), and individual subject's loss aversion coefficient (λ) fully mediated the correlation between GPT score and risky choice percentage across subjects (indirect effect: a × b = 0.024, 95% CI [0.007 0.045]; direct effect: c'=−0.003, 95% CI [−0.014 0.008]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Preacher and Hayes, 2008; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between model parameters and behavior.

claim: Individual subject's loss aversion coefficient (λ) fully mediated the correlation between GPT score and risky choice percentage across subjects (indirect effect: a × b = 0.024, 95% CI [0.007 0.045]; direct effect: c'=−0.003, 95% CI [−0.014 0.008]).
source: Furthermore, we found a significant negative correlation between loss aversion coefficient and the percentage of risky gamble choice across all trials (r = −0.919, p < 0.001), and individual subject's loss aversion coefficient (λ) fully mediated the correlation between GPT score and risky choice percentage across subjects (indirect effect: a × b = 0.024, 95% CI [0.007 0.045]; direct effect: c'=−0.003, 95% CI [−0.014 0.008]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Preacher and Hayes, 2008; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Subjects' greed personality traits were associated with their risky choice preference and loss aversion is the potential mediator for such effect.
source: Together, our behavioral results showed that subjects' greed personality traits were associated with their risky choice preference and suggested loss aversion as the potential mediator for such effect (Similar results were found in the behavioral replication study, see Figure 3—figure supplements 3–4).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the behavioral and mediation analyses.

claim: A neural network including bilateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), bilateral parietal cortex, and left posterior cingulate showed activities that positively correlated with potential gains of the gambles (z = 3.1, p < 0.05 FDR cluster correction).
source: Consistent with previous studies (Canessa et al., 2013; Park et al., 2011; Plassmann et al., 2010; Tom et al., 2007), we found a neural network including bilateral orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), bilateral parietal cortex, and left posterior cingulate, whose activities positively correlated with potential gains of the gambles (z = 3.1, p < 0.05 false discovery rate (FDR) cluster correction; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Brain activities in the right OFC, bilateral striatum, bilateral insula and bilateral inferior parietal gyrus were found negatively correlated with the magnitudes of the potential loss associated with the gamble (z = 3.1, p < 0.05 FDR correction).
source: Similarly, brain activities in the right OFC, bilateral striatum, bilateral insula and bilateral inferior parietal gyrus were found negatively correlated with the magnitudes of the potential loss associated with the gamble (z = 3.1, p < 0.05 FDR correction; Figure 4B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Conjunction analysis identified that the medial OFC (mOFC) activity was related to the representation of both gain and loss prospects of the gamble.
source: Furthermore, our conjunction analysis identified that the medial OFC (mOFC) activity was related to the representation of both gain and loss prospects of the gamble (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by conjunction analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Conjunction analysis revealed an overlapping area in the ventral striatum at a more lenient threshold (z = 2.3, p < 0.05 FDR correction).
source: Consistent with previous literature (Tom et al., 2007), this conjunction analysis also revealed an overlapping area in the ventral striatum, albeit at a more lenient threshold (z = 2.3, p < 0.05 FDR correction; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by conjunction analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neural loss aversion in the mOFC showed a significant positive correlation with behavioral loss aversion coefficients (ln (λ); r = 0.450, p = 0.024).
source: Indeed, neural loss aversion in the mOFC, defined as the difference between mOFC activities towards losses versus gains (-βloss - βgain) (Tom et al., 2007), showed a significant positive correlation with behavioral loss aversion coefficients (ln (λ); r = 0.450, p = 0.024) even after correction for potential outliers (robust regression, t = 2.203, p = 0.038; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neural loss aversion signal in the mOFC negatively correlated with individual subject's GPT score (r = -0.449, p = 0.028).
source: Moreover, as expected, such neural loss aversion signal also negatively correlated with individual subject's GPT score (r = -0.449, p = 0.028; robust regression, t = -2.239, p = 0.035), echoing our behavioral results of the association between GPT scores and behavioral loss aversion (ln (λ); r = -0.434, p = 0.034).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Activities in the ventral striatum did not exhibit significant correlation with behavioral loss aversion coefficients (ln (λ); r = -0.012, p = 0.954).
source: Finally, activities in the ventral striatum, also identified from conjunction analysis above, did not exhibit significant correlation with behavioral loss aversion coefficients (ln (λ); r = -0.012, p = 0.954) nor with GPT score (r = -0.239, p = 0.262).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of ventral striatum.

claim: Activities in the ventral striatum did not exhibit significant correlation with GPT score (r = -0.239, p = 0.262).
source: Finally, activities in the ventral striatum, also identified from conjunction analysis above, did not exhibit significant correlation with behavioral loss aversion coefficients (ln (λ); r = -0.012, p = 0.954) nor with GPT score (r = -0.239, p = 0.262).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of ventral striatum.

claim: The correlation between individual's trait-greed and behavioral loss aversion could be fully mediated by the neural loss aversion measures in the mOFC (indirect effect: a × b = −0.024, 95% CI [−0.084 –0.001]; direct effect: c'=−0.047, 95% CI [−0.117 0.024]).
source: Consistent with our prediction, we found the correlation between individual's trait-greed and behavioral loss aversion could be fully mediated by the neural loss aversion measures in the mOFC (indirect effect: a × b = −0.024, 95% CI [−0.084 –0.001]; direct effect: c'=−0.047, 95% CI [−0.117 0.024]), suggesting higher GPT score (greed personality trait) might lead to lower behavioral loss aversion (task performance) by engaging brain activities in the mOFC, which by itself is a pivotal structure involved in the integration of gain and loss prospects (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by mediation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Higher GPT score (greed personality trait) might lead to lower behavioral loss aversion (task performance) by engaging brain activities in the mOFC.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we found the correlation between individual's trait-greed and behavioral loss aversion could be fully mediated by the neural loss aversion measures in the mOFC (indirect effect: a × b = −0.024, 95% CI [−0.084 –0.001]; direct effect: c'=−0.047, 95% CI [−0.117 0.024]), suggesting higher GPT score (greed personality trait) might lead to lower behavioral loss aversion (task performance) by engaging brain activities in the mOFC, which by itself is a pivotal structure involved in the integration of gain and loss prospects (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mediation analysis results.

claim: mOFC is a pivotal structure involved in the integration of gain and loss prospects.
source: Consistent with our prediction, we found the correlation between individual's trait-greed and behavioral loss aversion could be fully mediated by the neural loss aversion measures in the mOFC (indirect effect: a × b = −0.024, 95% CI [−0.084 –0.001]; direct effect: c'=−0.047, 95% CI [−0.117 0.024]), suggesting higher GPT score (greed personality trait) might lead to lower behavioral loss aversion (task performance) by engaging brain activities in the mOFC, which by itself is a pivotal structure involved in the integration of gain and loss prospects (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mediation analysis and supported by the neuroimaging results.

claim: Insatiable appetite for more is associated with elevated impulsivity and novelty seeking, which are comorbid with obsessive gambling, substance and behavioral addiction and aberrant behavior in adolescence.
source: Indeed, insatiable appetite for more is associated with elevated impulsivity and novelty seeking, which are comorbid with obsessive gambling, substance and behavorial addiction and aberrant behavior in adolescence (Clark, 2014; Robbins and Clark, 2015; Seuntjens et al., 2015; Spear, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on impulsivity and addiction.

claim: Never satisfied with what one currently has could relate to risk-taking either by 'nudging' subjects into the loss domain and all the options are framed as potential or sure losses or by elevated attention to losses (loss aversion).
source: On the other hand, never satisfied with what one current has could relate to risk-taking either by 'nudging' subjects into the loss domain and all the options are framed as potential or sure losses or by elevated attention to losses (loss aversion) (De Martino et al., 2010; De Martino et al., 2009; Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2013; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2009; Thaler and Johnson, 1990).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to literature on loss aversion and framing effects.

claim: The study confirmed the association between greed personality trait and risk-taking in general.
source: By taking advantage of an experimental design that included gain, loss and mixed gambles, we not only confirmed the association between greed personality trait and risk-taking in general, but also had the opportunity to demonstrate such correlation was selectively mediated by individual's loss aversion, but not risk attitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings based on the experimental data.

claim: The correlation between greed personality trait and risk-taking was selectively mediated by individual's loss aversion, but not risk attitude.
source: By taking advantage of an experimental design that included gain, loss and mixed gambles, we not only confirmed the association between greed personality trait and risk-taking in general, but also had the opportunity to demonstrate such correlation was selectively mediated by individual's loss aversion, but not risk attitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's mediation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: BOLD responses in the mOFC, in addition to representing gain and loss prospects, encoded the neural loss aversion signal which in turn mediated the relationship between individual greed trait score and behavioral loss aversion coefficient.
source: In parallel, our neuroimaging results showed that BOLD responses in the mOFC, in addition to representing gain and loss prospects, encoded the neural loss aversion signal which in turn mediated the relationship between individual greed trait score and behavioral loss aversion coefficient (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a summary of the neuroimaging findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: The study's data provide a unique neural link to associate greed personality trait with subject's risk-taking behavior.
source: Therefore, our data provide a unique neural link to associate greed personality trait with subject's risk-taking behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined behavioral and neuroimaging findings.

claim: In the current task, greed scores did not correlate with subjects' risk attitude measurement.
source: Although it has been suggested that trait-greed might be directly related to risk attitude (Mussel et al., 2015), it is worth noting that in our task greed scores did not correlate with subjects' risk attitude measurement, and this result also corresponded well with a previous study showing that greed personality was not associated with risk seeking preference in the gain-only gambles (Seuntjens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Adolescents and young adults tend to have higher risk tolerance.
source: We reasoned that such discrepancy could be due to the fact that most of our subjects in the fMRI study were young adults (mean age: 21.360 years) and previous studies have suggested that adolescents and young adults tend to have higher risk tolerance (Barkley-Levenson and Galván, 2014; Grubb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on age and risk tolerance.

claim: The risk attitudes of young adults might cluster at the ceiling where the greed personality trait related effect on risk attitude is minimal.
source: Therefore, one possible explanation is that the risk attitudes of the young adults, whom most of our subjects were, might cluster at the ceiling where the greed personality trait related effect on risk attitude is minimal.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of correlation between GPT and risk attitude.

claim: Subjects tended to be risk neutral (mean = 1.033) instead of risk averse as commonly observed in other studies with similar experimental setups.
source: Indeed, prospect theory model estimated parameters showed that our subjects tended to be risk neutral (mean = 1.033) instead of risk averse as commonly observed in other studies with similar experimental setups (Suzuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the study's model-based analysis and comparison with other studies.

claim: Loss aversion is another critical factor influencing subjects' risk-taking, especially in the mixed gamble environment.
source: In the current study, we identified that mOFC, whose activity represented a 'neural loss aversion' signal, mediated the effect of greed personality on individual behavioral loss aversion. According to prospect theory, loss aversion is another critical factor influencing subjects' risk-taking, especially in the mixed gamble environment (Barkley-Levenson et al., 2013; Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; Köbberling and Wakker, 2005; Tversky and Kahneman, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prospect theory literature.

claim: Some studies revealed that sensitivity to losses was driven by negative emotions such as anxiety or fear, which was associated with elevated response in the amygdala, whereas gain processing was implemented in the activities of reward pathway structures such as ventral striatum.
source: For example, some studies revealed that sensitivity to losses was driven by negative emotions such as anxiety or fear, which was associated with elevated response in the amygdala, whereas gain processing was implemented in the activities of reward pathway structures such as ventral striatum (Camerer, 2005; De Martino et al., 2010; Sokol-Hessner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on the neural basis of loss aversion.

claim: Compared to healthy control subjects, unmedicated anxiety patients exhibited equivalent levels of loss aversion.
source: However, recent studies also found that compared to healthy control subjects, unmedicated anxiety patients exhibited equivalent levels of loss aversion (Charpentier et al., 2017), contradicting the interaction of distributed brain structure hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Charpentier et al., 2017.

claim: The subjective value of potential gains and losses might be encoded in the same brain regions, such as ventral striatum and mOFC/vmPFC, and the asymmetric activities towards gains and losses within these regions might compose the neural loss aversion signal.
source: The other line of research, however, suggested the possibility of encoding the subjective value of potential gains and losses in the same brain regions, such as ventral striatum and mOFC/ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and the asymmetric activities towards gains and losses within these regions might compose the neural loss aversion signal (Canessa et al., 2013; Tom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on neural encoding of subjective value.

claim: The OFC plays a pivotal role in processing rewards and punishments.
source: A variety of literatures have suggested that the OFC plays a pivotal role in processing rewards and punishments (Knutson et al., 2003; O'Doherty et al., 2001), making it well suited among the candidates of encoding a neural loss aversion signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on OFC function.

claim: BOLD responses in the mOFC were found to correlate with subjective (both appetitive and aversive) values of different modalities of stimuli, such as smell, snack foods, soda drinks and monetary gains and losses.
source: For instance, BOLD responses in the mOFC were found to correlate with subjective (both appetitive and aversive) values of different modalities of stimuli, such as smell (Gottfried et al., 2002), snack foods (Plassmann et al., 2010; Suzuki et al., 2017), soda drinks (McClure et al., 2004) and monetary gains and losses (De Martino et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on mOFC and subjective value.

claim: mOFC activity correlates with both potential gains and losses and the response asymmetry towards gains and losses in the mOFC was correlated with behavioral loss aversion.
source: Consistent with previous research, we also found mOFC activity correlates with both potential gains and losses and the response asymmetry towards gains and losses in the mOFC was correlated with behavioral loss aversion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the study's neuroimaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The neural loss aversion representation of mOFC mediated the effect of greed personality on behavioral loss aversion, providing additional support for the critical role of mOFC in integrating potential gains and losses and functioning as a neural network gateway to bias choice behavior.
source: Furthermore, this neural loss aversion representation of mOFC mediated the effect of greed personality on behavioral loss aversion (Figure 5), providing additional support for the critical role of mOFC in integrating potential gains and losses and functioning as a neural network gateway to bias choice behavior (Behrens et al., 2008; Kable and Glimcher, 2007; Kable and Glimcher, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the study's mediation analysis and citations to literature on mOFC function.

claim: With a more lenient threshold (z = 2.3, p < 0.05 FDR correction), activities in the ventral striatum were observed that correlated with both gains and losses.
source: With a more lenient threshold (z = 2.3, p < 0.05 FDR correction), we also observed activities in the ventral striatum that correlated with both gains and losses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by neuroimaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ROI analysis didn't yield a significant correlation between ventral striatum activity and behavioral loss aversion, potentially due to the difference in the experimental designs.
source: However, unlike previous research, our ROI analysis didn't yield a significant correlation between ventral striatum activity and behavioral loss aversion, potentially due to the difference in the experimental designs (Canessa et al., 2013; Tom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on the study's data analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: In the current task, options were presented as the two-alternative choice selection task, in contrast to the default option accept and reject task used in earlier studies.
source: Indeed, in our task, options were presented as the two-alternative choice selection task, in contrast to the default option accept and reject task used in earlier studies (Tom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: There has been evidence suggesting the way options were presented and framed might have a peculiar effect on value representation and subsequently behavioral risk-taking.
source: There has been evidence suggesting the way options were presented and framed might have a peculiar effect on value representation and subsequently behavioral risk-taking (Boureau and Dayan, 2011; De Martino et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on framing effects.

claim: Greed is a multi-faceted personality trait and may manifest as a myriad of behavioral propensities under different contexts.
source: Finally, it is worth emphasizing that greed is a multi-faceted personality trait and may manifest as a myriad of behavioral propensities under different contexts.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of greed as a personality trait.

claim: Greed might be tied to subjects' attitude towards ambiguity, the uncertainty of risk itself, or to asymmetrical updating of positive and negative outcomes.
source: For example, greed might be tied to subjects' attitude towards ambiguity, the uncertainty of risk itself, or to asymmetrical updating of positive and negative outcomes (Grubb et al., 2016; Hsu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential relationships, supported by citations.

claim: 76 university students (18–29 years old, mean = 22.513, s.d. = 2.625; 46 females) participated in the pilot study.
source: To confirm the correlation between greed personality and impulsivity personality, we ran a pilot study of 76 university students (18–29 years old, mean = 22.513, s.d. = 2.625; 46 females) who were asked to complete the online versions of both the greed and impulsivity personality trait questionnaires.
evidence: This is a description of the pilot study sample.

claim: 28 healthy adult subjects took part in the fMRI experiment.
source: Another 28 healthy adult subjects took part in the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the fMRI study sample.

claim: Three subjects were excluded from data analysis due to either falling asleep during scanning (one subject) or misunderstanding of task instructions (two subjects), leaving 25 subjects (18–26 years old, mean = 21.360, s.d. = 2.158; 11 females) for both behavioral and imaging data analyses.
source: Three subjects were excluded from data analysis due to either falling asleep during scanning (one subject) or misunderstanding of task instructions (two subjects), leaving 25 subjects (18–26 years old, mean = 21.360, s.d. = 2.158; 11 females) for both behavioral and imaging data analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the final fMRI study sample after exclusions.

claim: A behavioral replication study recruited 51 subjects to complete both the personality questionnaires and the risky decision task after the fMRI experiment.
source: Additionally, we ran a behavioral replication study by recruiting another 51 subjects to complete both the personality questionnaires and the risky decision task after the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the replication study sample.

claim: Two subjects who chose risky gambles less than 10% of all trials were excluded from data analysis, leaving 49 subjects (18–25 years old, mean = 21.200, s.d. = 2.061; 25 females) for further data analyses.
source: Two subjects who chose risky gambles less than 10% of all trials were excluded from data analysis, leaving 49 subjects (18–25 years old, mean = 21.200, s.d. = 2.061; 25 females) for further data analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the final replication study sample after exclusions.

claim: All subjects reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders and no current use of any psychoactive medications and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
source: All subjects reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders and no current use of any psychoactive medications and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
evidence: This is a description of the inclusion criteria for subjects.

claim: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University (2017-11-01).
source: This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the School of Psychological and Cognitive Sciences, Peking University (2017-11-01).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The 7-item Dispositional Greed Scale (DGS) was used to measure individual differences in trait-greed.
source: The 7-item Dispositional Greed Scale (DGS) was used to measure individual differences in trait-greed (Mussel et al., 2018; Seuntjens et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the measurement tool used.

claim: A 5-point scale was used to rate each item in the DGS with a response format ranging from 1 'strongly disagree' to 5 'strongly agree'.
source: A 5-point scale was used to rate each item with a response format ranging from 1 'strongly disagree' to 5 'strongly agree'.
evidence: This is a description of the rating scale used.

claim: The total scores on the DGS can range from 7 to 35, and a higher score indicates a higher level of greed personality.
source: The total scores can range from 7 to 35, and a higher score indicates a higher level of greed personality.
evidence: This is a description of the scoring system for the DGS.

claim: Impulsivity personality was evaluated using the Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11).
source: Impulsivity personality was evaluated using the popular Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS-11) (Patton et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a description of the measurement tool used.

claim: The BIS-11 with 30 items was divided into three subscales: cognitive, motor, and non-planning.
source: The trait scale (BIS-11) with 30 items was divided into three subscales: cognitive, motor, and non-planning.
evidence: This is a description of the structure of the BIS-11.

claim: Each item in the BIS-11 is rated on a 5-point frequency scale ranging from 'almost never' to 'almost always' with higher scores indicating higher levels of impulsiveness trait.
source: Each item is rated on a 5-point frequency scale ranging from 'almost never' to 'almost always' with higher scores indicating higher levels of impulsiveness trait.
evidence: This is a description of the rating scale for the BIS-11.

claim: During the fMRI experiment, all subjects completed a gambling task with 230 trials of four different types: gain, loss, mixed and catch trials.
source: During the fMRI experiment, all subjects completed a gambling task with 230 trials of four different types: gain, loss, mixed and catch trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: In the gain condition (40 trials), subjects were asked to choose between a certain reward (¥1 to ¥ 15) and a gamble with equal probabilities of receiving zero or a reward with varying magnitudes (¥ 3 to ¥ 30).
source: In the gain condition (40 trials), subjects were asked to choose between a certain reward (¥1 to ¥ 15) and a gamble with equal probabilities of receiving zero or a reward with varying magnitudes (¥ 3 to ¥ 30).
evidence: This is a description of the gain trials in the experimental task.

claim: In the 40 loss trials, the signs of gamble and certain option amounts in the gain condition were flipped.
source: In the 40 loss trials, we simply flipped the signs of gamble and certain option amounts in the gain condition.
evidence: This is a description of the loss trials in the experimental task.

claim: In the 144 mixed trials, subjects were asked to choose between a guaranteed amount of zero and a gamble with equal probabilities of a gain (¥ 8 to ¥ 30, in increments of ¥ 2) and a loss (¥ 5 to ¥ 27, in increments of ¥ 2).
source: In the 144 mixed trials, subjects were asked to choose between a guaranteed amount of zero and a gamble with equal probabilities of a gain (¥ 8 to ¥ 30, in increments of ¥ 2) and a loss (¥ 5 to ¥ 27, in increments of ¥ 2).
evidence: This is a description of the mixed trials in the experimental task.

claim: Six catch trials (three in the gain frame and three in the loss frame) were added where there existed objectively optimal choices to ensure that subjects remained actively engaged in the task.
source: Finally, to ensure that subjects remained actively engaged in the task, we added six catch trials (three in the gain frame and three in the loss frame) where there existed objectively optimal choices (For example: 50% chance of ¥ 10 versus ¥ 10 for sure).
evidence: This is a description of the catch trials in the experimental task.

claim: All the subjects made correct choices for the catch trials, suggesting continued engagement throughout the experiment.
source: All the subjects made correct choices for these catch trials, suggesting continued engagement throughout the experiment.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral data from the catch trials.

claim: The sequence of all 230 trials, as well as gamble/certain option location (left versus right) on the screen, was randomized across subjects and trials were divided into two equal sessions.
source: The sequence of all 230 trials, as well as gamble/certain option location (left versus right) on the screen, was randomized across subjects and trials were divided into two equal sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Subjects were instructed to respond within 5 s after the choice options were revealed on the screen.
source: In each trial, subjects were instructed to respond within 5 s after the choice options were revealed on the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the task instructions.

claim: Subjects responded with reaction time (RT) of 2.013 ± 0.382 s (mean ±s.d.) for each trial.
source: Subjects responded with reaction time (RT) of 2.013 ± 0.382 s (mean ±s.d.) for each trial.
evidence: This is based on the behavioral data from the experiment.

claim: A randomly jittered inter-trial interval (ITI) with a mean of 6 s (range: 4–8 s) was introduced before the beginning of next trial.
source: A randomly jittered inter-trial interval (ITI) with a mean of 6 s (range: 4–8 s) was introduced before the beginning of next trial (see experiment procedure in Figure 1 and gamble sets in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each subject was endowed with ¥30 at the beginning of the experiment (maximum amount subjects could have lost in any single trial).
source: Each subject was endowed with ¥30 at the beginning of the experiment (maximum amount subjects could have lost in any single trial), and was told that one randomly selected trial at the end of the experiment would be played for real money to enforce incentive compatibility.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: One randomly selected trial at the end of the experiment would be played for real money to enforce incentive compatibility.
source: Each subject was endowed with ¥30 at the beginning of the experiment (maximum amount subjects could have lost in any single trial), and was told that one randomly selected trial at the end of the experiment would be played for real money to enforce incentive compatibility.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: All the subjects received a ¥90 subject fee upon completion of the study and they on average earned ¥124 at the end of the experiment.
source: All the subjects also received a ¥90 subject fee upon completion of the study and they on average earned ¥124 at the end of the experiment.
evidence: This is based on the payment data from the experiment.

claim: The correlation between the magnitudes of potential gain and loss in the gamble option was not significant across trials (r = 0.011, p = 0.867).
source: By design, the correlation between the magnitudes of potential gain and loss in the gamble option was not significant across trials (r = 0.011, p = 0.867), allowing us to investigate their corresponding neural activities separately.
evidence: This is based on the experimental design and statistical analysis.

claim: Hierarchical Bayesian analysis (HBA) approach was used in model fitting to obtain the estimated model parameters for individual subjects.
source: We took the hierarchical Bayesian analysis (HBA) approach in model fitting to obtain the estimated model parameters for individual subjects (Ahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical method used.

claim: Bayesian model comparison analysis using deviance information criteria (DIC) showed that the different risk attitudes model did not perform significantly better than the single risk attitude model: the protected exceedance probability (PXP) was 0.539 and the Bayesian omnibus risk (BOR) indicator was 0.796.
source: Bayeisan model comparison analysis using deviance information criteria (DIC) showed that the different risk attitudes model (Equation 4) did not perform significantly better than the single risk attitude model: the protected exceedance probability (PXP) was 0.539 and the Bayesian omnibus risk (BOR) indicator measuring the probability that all model frequencies are indistinguishable (0 indicates the models are well distinguishable, and 1 means the models are indistinguishable) was 0.796 (Spiegelhalter et al., 2014; Rigoux et al., 2014; Stephan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on Bayesian model comparison analysis.

claim: Whole-brain image collection was performed using a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner with a 64-channel head coil at the Center for MRI Research of Peking University.
source: Whole-brain image collection was performed using a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner with a 64-channel head coil at the Center for MRI Research of Peking University.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging equipment and location.

claim: All image data preprocessing and analyses were implemented with SPM12.
source: All image data preprocessing and analyses were implemented with SPM12 (Wellcome Trust Center for Neuroimaging).
evidence: This is a description of the software used for analysis.

claim: All results are whole-brain corrected for multiple comparison by reporting brain activities surviving a voxel-level uncorrected threshold of p<0.001 and then a cluster-level false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of p<0.05.
source: All results are whole-brain corrected for multiple comparison by reporting brain activities surviving a voxel-level uncorrected threshold of p<0.001 and then a cluster-level false discovery rate (FDR) threshold of p<0.05 (Rouam, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical correction method used.

claim: The neural loss aversion at the ROI for individual subject was calculated by subtracting the GLM parameter estimators of potential gains from those of the losses (-βloss - βgain).
source: The neural loss aversion at the ROI for individual subject was calculated by subtracting the GLM parameter estimators of potential gains from those of the losses (-βloss - βgain) (Tom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the calculation method, supported by a citation.

claim: Mediation analysis was carried out using statistical package 'PROCESS' in SPSS.
source: We carried out mediation analysis using statistical package 'PROCESS' in SPSS (http://processmacro.org/index.html) (Preacher and Hayes, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical tool used.

claim: The 95% bias corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) of the indirect effect were calculated on the basis of 5000 bootstrap samples.
source: The 95% bias corrected bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) of the indirect effect were calculated on the basis of 5000 bootstrap samples.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used.
